name: Suusamyr Valley
near: Kaysar — ~4.9 km in a straight line from the catalogue point (OSM); the valley also has the villages of Suusamyr and Kojomkul (the Kojomkul mazar (shrine) and museum — too.kg, eurasia.travel).
elev: Average elevation — about 2,200–2,300 m (eurasia.travel, too.kg); in different parts of the valley — 2,000–3,200 m (Trip to Kyrgyzstan); the surrounding peaks — up to 4,500 m.
short: Suusamyr is a high-mountain valley ~155 km long and up to 40 km wide at ~2,200 m between the Kyrgyz, Talas and Suusamyr ranges: the country's best pastures, yurts, kumys and the Bishkek — Osh highway.
desc: The Suusamyr Valley is an intermontane basin of the Inner Tian Shan in the Jayyl district of the Chuy region, about 160 km southwest of Bishkek. Its length is around 150–155 km, its width up to 40 km, and its average elevation 2,200–2,300 m. The Suusamyr and West Karakol rivers flow through the valley and merge to form the Kokomeren. In summer it is a “green sea” of tall-grass pastures — some of the best in the country: shepherds set up yurts and make kumys and ayran, and kumys-therapy sanatoriums operate; in winter there is deep snow and severe frost, and a ski base operates near the Too-Ashuu Pass. There are more than 300 plant species here and snow leopards live in the area; burial mounds and stone statues (from the 6th century BC) have survived. In the village of Kojomkul there is the mazar (shrine) of the legendary hero Kojomkul with handprints, and a museum. In 1992 the valley was shaken by the strong Suusamyr earthquake (M≈7.3).
guide: Suusamyr is best seen right after the Too-Ashuu tunnel: the valley opens up below as a green carpet to the horizon. In summer stop at the yurts along the highway and try fresh kumys — here it is considered one of the best in the country. If you have a day, turn off to the village of Kojomkul to see the hero's mazar with its “handprints” and the local museum. It is cold at night in the valley even in July (2,200 m), so bring warm clothes if you're staying overnight in a yurt camp. In early summer locals pick steppe mushrooms here, and paragliders catch the thermals above the treeless slopes.
see: The panorama of the valley from the descent after the Too-Ashuu tunnel; summer pastures with yurts and herds; the confluence of the Suusamyr and West Karakol (the source of the Kokomeren); the Kojomkul mazar and museum in the village of the same name; burial mounds and stone statues; the Too-Ashuu ski base in winter.
skip: You're not driving the Bishkek — Osh highway or heading to Talas — 2.5 h one way specifically for the valley is only justified with a night in a yurt. You expect “sights” — the main thing here is open space and pastures. You're travelling in late autumn/winter without winter tyres.
diff: Easy: most of it is accessible from the paved highway, and walks across the pastures involve no elevation gain. Keep in mind the altitude of ~2,200 m (cool, and some people feel slightly short of breath). Side dirt roads to the pastures depend on the weather and sometimes require an SUV.
when: May–July — the “green sea” of pastures (eurasia.travel); June–September — the yurt and kumys season; early summer — mushrooms. In winter (December–March) — snow, severe frost and skiing at Too-Ashuu; the highway is open, but restrictions are possible during snowfall (24.kg, 02.2026).
hours: Open natural area, open 24 hours; the Bishkek — Osh highway runs year-round with temporary restrictions in bad weather. Yurt camps — mostly in summer (Turan Camp is advertised as operating all year).
daytime: Morning and evening — soft light over the pastures and less wind; in summer thunderstorms are possible by day. It is cold at night even in summer (editorial note, from the ~2,200 m altitude).
how: From Bishkek along the Bishkek — Osh highway through Kara-Balta and the tunnel at the Too-Ashuu Pass (~150–160 km, about 2–2.5 h; rome2rio — 153 km, 2 h 17 min). Marshrutkas (minibuses) and shared taxis towards Suusamyr, Talas, Toktogul and Osh leave from Bishkek's bus stations (too.kg).
needcar: Yes: the valley is 2+ h from Bishkek and very extended — you need a car, a taxi or intercity transport. Getting around within the valley without a car is difficult.
self: Yes: by car or by intercity marshrutka/taxi; yurt camps and guesthouses accept guests without a tour. There is mobile coverage in the valley.
roadtype: The paved Bishkek — Osh highway crosses the valley; side roads to the villages are partly paved, and to the pastures dirt (the surface type is not uniform by section).
traveltime: Bishkek → Suusamyr: ~2 h 15 min — 2.5 h by car (rome2rio 153 km; too.kg/eurasia — 160 km). From the Too-Ashuu tunnel to the central part of the valley — 15–20 min.
stay: Turan Camp ethno-camp (Suusamyr village): double yurt 4,000 som, upgraded 6,000 som, four-bed 8,000 som per night with breakfast, kumys, horse rides, archery range (meiman.kg, 2026; +996 550 993 993). Guesthouses, cafés and shops in the valley villages (too.kg); the Too-Ashuu ski base (66 beds + cottages, asiamixtravel); kumys-therapy sanatoriums in summer.
net: Too.kg: there is mobile coverage throughout the valley; on remote pastures and on the pass the coverage may drop out. The operator is not specified.
entry: There is no entrance fee for the valley. What you pay for is passage through the highway tunnels (50 som for a Kyrgyz-registered passenger car / 200 som for a foreign one, since 01.01.2024) and camp services.
transfer: Shared taxi Bishkek — Osh 2,500 som per seat (2026; to Suusamyr it is cheaper — price not confirmed); taxi $19–24 according to rome2rio; tunnel fee 50 som/car. Marshrutka fares to Suusamyr were not found.
bring: Warm clothes even in summer (2,200 m, cold nights), a rain jacket, sun protection (open pastures), cash for kumys and yurts; get water in the villages — drinking river water is not recommended (too.kg). In winter — winter tyres and a reserve of fuel.
warn: In winter — severe frost, snowfall and restrictions on the Too-Ashuu Pass (24.kg 13.02.2026). Don't drink river water (livestock graze there). A seismically active zone (1992 earthquake). On the pastures — shepherds' dogs; don't approach herds without their owners. At an altitude of ~2,200 m it is cool and the sun is harsh.
food: Kumys is the main gastronomic highlight: shepherds make it on the summer jailoo (pastures), and kumys-therapy sanatoriums operate (too.kg, eurasia.travel); ayran; Kyrgyz cuisine in roadside yurts and cafés along the highway; at Turan Camp — breakfast included, lunch and dinner from the menu.
reviews: Google Maps (Susamyr Valley): 4.8/5, 41 ratings (03.10.2026). Traveller reviews (YouTube, blogs): pros — endless pastures, kumys, “the most beautiful road in Kyrgyzstan”; cons — cold at night, simple service, long distances.
p.sum: Suusamyr is a high-mountain jailoo (summer pasture) valley (~2,200 m) 2–2.5 h from Bishkek beyond the Too-Ashuu Pass; the Bishkek — Osh highway runs straight through it. It is most convenient with your own car (tunnel fee 50/200 som) or with a tour. Without a car — a marshrutka or a seat-by-seat taxi towards Osh/Talas/Toktogul, getting off in the valley (to Osh a seat costs 2,500 som, to Suusamyr it is cheaper, but the exact fare was not found). In summer (June–September) yurts selling kumys stand along the highway (a litre nationwide costs 200–350 som, 2026). You can stay overnight at the Turan Camp ethno-camp (yurt 4,000–8,000 som with breakfast, horses, archery), the Altai guesthouse in Suusamyr village or Suus Lodge (double room $40). In winter there are frosts down to −30 and skiing at Too-Ashuu.

p.budget.economy: ≈2,000–4,000 som: taxi/marshrutka seat one way (fare to Suusamyr not found; rough guide — a part of the Bishkek — Osh price of 800–2,500 som), kumys 200–350 som/L, lunch 300–500 som
p.budget.comfort: Own car or a tour (€384 per group) + a night at Turan Camp 4,000–8,000 som per yurt with breakfast; Suus Lodge from $40 for a double room
p.permits: Not needed. Only the Bishkek — Osh tunnel passage is paid (50/200 som)
p.access: Good for children and older people: everything can be seen from the highway, with yurts by the road. With a wheelchair — roadside cafés and camps (dirt). At an altitude of ~2,200 m it is cool and the sun is strong. With a dog — be careful near herds and shepherd dogs
